newsitem.title: UK: Dlr ends European session mixed, below 1.69 marks.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends European session mixed, below 1.69 marks.

text.p: 1638 GMT - Dlr ends European session mixed, touch softer and below 1.69 marks, shade up and just below 123 yen amid expectations of 25 bp Fed funds rate hike at Tuesday's FOMC. Buba's Welteke says current German rates appropriate but rise in U.S. rates would push them up, which "not desirable". Stg off high after robust data, mark mixed on crosses though off lows.
The dollar was firm but off peaks in late Europe as the buoyant market became wary that a rise in U.S. rates on Tuesday could trigger a selloff in U.S. stocks and bonds.
"It is hard to see what the upside for the dollar will be, but I think the currency will wait for a lead from the bond and equity markets," said Chris Turner, currency strategist at BZW.

While the dollar has been propped up by widespread expectations the Federal Reserve will raise key rates on Tuesday for the first time in two years, stock and bond markets have been less enthusiastic.

"Markets are beginning to realise that maybe stock and bond markets will not react so well if there is a change in the direction of monetary policy," said Ernesto Ramirez, European economist at Bankers Trust.
"When the U.S. tightens, it reinforces the view that in Europe there might be a turning point sometime this year and also Japan might be tempted to follow course," Ramirez said.
The Federal Reserve Open Market Committee (FOMC) meets on Tuesday to consider monetary policy.
At 1601 GMT the dollar stood at 1.6878/83 marks, little changed against 1.6876/81 in late Europe on Friday.
Earlier, the dollar scaled to peaks of 1.6930 marks. Against the yen, the dollar jumped to session highs of 123.17 yen in Europe before ending the session little changed at 122.68 yen.
Bets for a rise in U.S. rates deepened last Thursday after Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan stressed the importance of a rate hike to tame inflation.

A Reuters poll of 48 economists, after Greenspan's remarks, showed 34 expected the Fed to raise its federal funds target to at least 5.50 percent from 5.25 percent. The funds rate,at which banks lend to each other on an overnight basis, was changed in Jan 96 when it was lowered by quarter point to 5.25 percent.

Analysts say the reason the dollar is so vulnerable to the reaction of the bond market is because of the amount of foreign investment in dollar securities, which are needed to fund the huge U.S. current account deficit. When these funds retrench from volatile U.S. asset markets, the dollar shivers.

"I expect the initial reaction of the dollar to a tightening will be a small drop. But the interest-rate differential argument will still last for the second-quarter of the year and it will still be favourable for dollar-Europe," said Ramirez.
Meanwhile, the German mark was mixed on its European crosses with trading patchy ahead of the FOMC meet.
Sterling ended the session firm but off peaks after a boost from robust UK current account data.
At 1622 GMT sterling stood at 2.7255 marks against 2.7038/48 in late Europe on Friday and against the dollar, sterling stood at $1.6130/40 against $1.6020/30 in late Europe on Friday.
